title: Mudurnu & Göynük: Quiet Silk Road Timber Towns Between Istanbul & Ankara

metaDescription: Explore Mudurnu and Göynük between Istanbul and Ankara. See Ottoman hammams, clock towers, Lake Abant and Lake Sünnet routes, and restored konaks.
quickAnswer: Mudurnu and Göynük are two Cittaslow Ottoman timber towns tucked into forested Bolu valleys roughly halfway between Istanbul and Ankara. Sitting 52 km apart along a scenic Silk Road corridor, they pair easily with Lake Abant and Lake Sünnet for a calm two-day drive featuring 14th-century hammams, wooden clock towers, and restored Ottoman konaks.

body.text: Why are Mudurnu and Göynük ideal stops on an Istanbul–Ankara drive?

Both towns sit less than an hour off the main TEM (O-4) motorway connecting Istanbul and Ankara, letting drivers swap highway service plazas for quiet valleys lined with whitewashed Ottoman timber houses. As members of [Cittaslow Türkiye](https://cittaslowturkiye.org/en/), Mudurnu and Göynük prioritize pedestrian heritage streets, local bakeries, and small workshops over tour-bus commercialization.

Historically, caravans traveling between Constantinople and Central Anatolia crossed these mountain passes, leaving behind merchant inns, guild halls, and endowments. Mudurnu holds a place on the [UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6038/) as a Historic Guild Town where the 700-year-old Ahi Merchants' Prayer (Esnaf Duası) is still recited every Friday morning in the old bazaar. From Istanbul's Asian side, reaching Göynük via Adapazarı and Taraklı takes roughly 3 hours (225 km), while Mudurnu lies about 2.5 hours (200 km) west of Ankara.
Which historic hammams, clock towers and mansions survive?

Mudurnu preserves the 1382 Yıldırım Bayezid Mosque and its twin-domed Ottoman hammam, an 1890 hillside clock tower, and monumental 19th-century mansions such as Armutçular and Keyvanlar Konağı. Göynük counters with more than 100 protected timber residences, the 14th-century Gazi Süleyman Paşa Mosque and Hammam, Akşemseddin's Tomb, and the 1923 wooden Zafer Kulesi (Victory Tower).

Because both towns were designated urban conservation areas before modern concrete expansion took hold, their historic cores remain compact and walkable ([Cittaslow Göynük Profile](https://cittaslowturkiye.org/tr/cittaslow-adaylari-goynuk-bolu/)). In Mudurnu, walk from Yıldırım Bayezid Mosque through the restored Demirci (Blacksmiths') and Arasta lanes before climbing the steps to the stone clock tower for valley views. In Göynük, visit the tomb of Akşemseddin—spiritual mentor to Sultan Mehmed II—browse boxwood spoon carvers along the stream, and climb to Zafer Kulesi before sunset.
How do you pair them with Lake Abant and Lake Sünnet?

Drive the natural loop connecting Bolu's highlands with both heritage towns: start at Lake Abant Nature Park, continue 20 km south (25 minutes) into Mudurnu for lunch and the historic bazaar, then follow the forested mountain road 28 km southwest to Lake Sünnet before descending 25 km into Göynük for the night.

This sequence keeps daily driving under two hours while contrasting pine-rimmed alpine lakes with timber streetscapes. Lake Abant offers a flat seven-kilometer lakeside path popular on weekends, whereas Lake Sünnet—formed by a historic landslide in a deep narrow valley—stays quiet even in summer and suits a coffee break or short lakeside walk.

body.text: Where can you stay in restored Ottoman konaks?

Both towns offer family-operated boutique stays inside 19th-century timber mansions featuring carved wood ceilings, sedir window benches, and home-cooked Bolu breakfasts. In Mudurnu, Hacı Şakirler Konağı, Tekkeliler Konağı, and Yarışkaşı Konağı sit steps from the old bazaar; in Göynük, Akşemseddin Konağı and Müderrisoğlu Konağı place guests right beside the historic stream and mosque complex.

Rooms in genuine historic konaks are smaller than standard chain hotels and often involve narrow wooden staircases without elevators, so check ground-floor availability if traveling with heavy luggage or mobility needs. Book ahead for Friday and Saturday nights in May, June, and October, when Istanbul and Ankara weekenders fill the limited room count.

items: Plan Mudurnu for Friday morning if you want to witness the weekly Ahi Merchants' Prayer in the bazaar.
Refuel near Bolu or Adapazarı before entering the winding forest road between Lake Sünnet and Göynük.
Pack a light jacket even in July; Bolu's mountain valleys drop noticeably in temperature after dusk.
Try regional keşli cevizli erişte (hand-cut noodles with dried yogurt cheese and walnuts) and Mudurnu's saray helvası.
Carry small Turkish lira bills for village produce stands, wooden spoon workshops, and national park gate fees.

faq.q: Can you visit both Mudurnu and Göynük in a single day?
faq.a: Yes, if you have a car. The two towns sit 52 km apart (about one hour via Lake Sünnet), so you can explore Mudurnu in the morning, stop briefly at Lake Sünnet, and walk Göynük in the afternoon before continuing to Istanbul or Ankara.

faq.q: Are the roads between Lake Abant, Mudurnu, and Göynük safe in winter?
faq.a: They are paved two-lane mountain roads, but snow and black ice are common from December through March. Winter tires are mandatory in Türkiye during winter months, and chains are advisable during heavy Bolu snowfall.

faq.q: Which town is better for an overnight stay: Mudurnu or Göynük?
faq.a: Göynük feels slightly more unified visually, with its hillside timber houses and illuminated Zafer Kulesi, while Mudurnu has stronger living guild traditions and quicker access to Lake Abant. Staying in Göynük works well if driving from Istanbul; Mudurnu suits trips starting from Ankara.

faq.q: Is Mudurnu's Yıldırım Bayezid Hammam still open for bathing?
faq.a: Yes, the historic 14th-century hammam has undergone restoration and operates as a functioning bathhouse with separate sections, though hours can shift seasonally—confirm locally upon arrival.

faq.q: Can you reach Mudurnu or Göynük by public transport?
faq.a: Direct intercity buses are limited. Travelers without a car take a bus to Bolu Otogar and transfer to local district minibuses, which makes pairing both towns and the lakes difficult in a short trip. A rental car or private driver is far more practical.

faq.q: What local crafts are worth buying in Mudurnu and Göynük?
faq.a: In Göynük, look for hand-carved boxwood spoons and tokalı örtü woven cotton headscarves. In Mudurnu, copperwork, needle lace (oya), and local saray helvası sweets are traditional specialties.
